slides.title: Dominance emerges from changes in social behavior
body: Crayfish _Procambarus clarkii_ establish **dominance**, a relationship in which one animal persistently attacks or approaches while the other withdraws. **Agonistic behavior** comprises conflict-related actions, including threats, grappling, attacks, retreats and escapes. Rank is assigned from these interactions rather than from posture alone.

Herberholz and colleagues paired previously isolated juveniles of similar size for 30 min. Synchronized recordings identified an abrupt transition: the future subordinate stopped repeated offensive actions and began retreating or escaping from its opponent.

A hierarchy therefore changes the selection of actions within an encounter. The behavioral transition establishes which animal yields under these conditions, but it does not identify the transmitter or neuronal change responsible. Animals could occasionally reengage after the initial decision, so dominance was assessed across the interaction.

slides.title: Electrical fields identify activity during free movement
body: Herberholz and colleagues recorded **field potentials**, changes in voltage in the water surrounding freely moving crayfish. Large, coordinated neuronal and muscle currents generate these signals, allowing neural pathway activation to be associated with observed behavior.

Bath electrodes at opposite ends of a 9.5 cm aquarium recorded activity while high-speed video sampled movement every 5 ms. Preliminary recordings compared the bath signal with signals from implanted electrodes in the same animal. Corresponding waveforms supported identification without retaining electrode leads during paired encounters.

The method preserved movement and contact between opponents. Waveform similarity validates particular escape signatures; it does not resolve every small neuron contributing to a field potential. Video supplied the animal’s identity and movement trajectory, preventing a voltage event from being classified solely by amplitude.

slides.title: Offensive tail flips prolong contact with an opponent
body: A **tail flip** is rapid abdominal flexion that moves a crayfish through water. During escape it separates the animal from a threat; during an **offensive tail flip**, the animal maintains its grip on the opponent and pulls it upward or over.

Herberholz and colleagues identified offensive movements using synchronized video and electrical recordings during juvenile encounters. Their abdominal movements began more slowly than ordinary escape flexion and were resolved across successive 5-ms video frames. These events were common during vigorous grappling.

An offensive movement therefore cannot be assigned an escape function merely because the abdomen flexes. Its electrical signature lacked the large initial giant-pathway response. The authors proposed a distinct motor circuit, but did not identify all of its neurons or prove that it was completely independent of nongiant escape circuitry.

slides.title: Retreat increases after the hierarchy is decided
body: The transition to subordinate status redistributes behavior rather than simply reducing all movement. Herberholz and colleagues aligned paired encounters to the first tail flip and counted attacks, approaches and retreats in successive 5-min periods.

Dominants maintained attacks and approaches while subordinates produced repeated retreats and escapes. Aggressive activity then declined across the 30-min observation, reaching roughly 15% of its initial level. Defensive actions fell as approaches and attacks became less frequent.

The temporal association links defensive behavior to the opponent’s actions and the established relationship. It does not establish that a fall in one escape reflex caused retreat, because retreat and different forms of escape recruit different circuits. An animal can suppress one stereotyped response while increasing another defensive action, especially when threats remain predictable during repeated encounters.

slides.title: Serotonin prolongs fighting in an established subordinate
body: **Serotonin**, or 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT), is a monoamine, a small amine-containing signaling molecule that can change neuronal responsiveness. A **neuromodulator** alters how a circuit responds to its inputs rather than necessarily triggering one fixed action. Huber and colleagues infused serotonin into freely moving _Astacus astacus_.

The treated subordinate was about 30% smaller than its opponent. After rank formation, 30 min of saline infusion preceded 60 min of serotonin delivery. Estimated circulating serotonin approached 10 µM. Fight duration and intensity increased to approximately three times their pretreatment levels.

Fighting returned toward baseline within 30 min after infusion ended. The saline phase controlled for infusion and time in the apparatus. These results establish a pharmacological increase in fighting persistence, but not that endogenous serotonin concentration alone determines rank or reverses physical superiority.

slides.title: Longer fighting reflects a reduced tendency to withdraw
body: Fighting intensity and duration are coupled: encounters that continue longer have more opportunity to escalate. Huber and colleagues therefore separated persistence from which animal initiated an encounter, the escalation sequence and which animal ultimately retreated.

During the 60-min serotonin infusion, duration accounted for most of the behavioral change. Subordinates continued contesting interactions longer, while the original opponent usually retained the eventual advantage. The saline and postinfusion periods provided within-pair comparisons.

The result supports a reduced likelihood of withdrawal during an ongoing interaction. It does not establish increased muscular strength, a reversal of hierarchy or a single general aggression pathway. Applied serotonin changed one component of the animal’s behavior under a particular asymmetry of body size, and that component must be distinguished from the final outcome.

slides.title: Giant pathways generate different escape trajectories
body: The **lateral giant** (LG) and **medial giant** (MG) are large interneurons that recruit stereotyped escape movements. An **interneuron** connects neurons within the nervous system; a **command neuron** can trigger an organized action when it fires. LG responds chiefly to abrupt abdominal input, whereas MG responds to anterior stimulation.

Herberholz and colleagues compared sharp mechanical stimuli with synchronized recordings. At 25 ms after movement onset, LG tail flips averaged about 99° relative to the animal’s forward axis, whereas MG movements averaged about 155°.

Both pathways produced a giant spike followed about 1.4 ms later by a large motor-related field potential. Their distinct trajectories and electrical signatures supported classification. These calibrated responses identify pathway recruitment, but the threshold for releasing a movement can still depend on ongoing behavior and social experience.

slides.title: Most social escapes recruit nongiant circuitry
body: **Nongiant escape** recruits interneurons and motor neurons without firing the giant command pathways. It produces more variable movements and also contributes to repeated swimming tail flips after an initial escape. A motor neuron carries neural output to muscle.

During 30-min juvenile encounters, Herberholz and colleagues observed extensive nongiant escape and swimming in the new subordinate. LG firing occurred only once across their paired encounters, when an opponent directly struck the subordinate’s abdomen. MG responses were concentrated during vigorous interaction.

Frequent defensive movement therefore does not imply frequent LG activation. Field potentials lacking the giant spike and large initial motor signature distinguished nongiant responses. The observed recruitment pattern supports selective control of escape pathways, but it cannot by itself determine whether serotonergic modulation or another signal changed their excitability.

slides.title: A stimulus threshold measures reflex availability
body: A **stimulus threshold** is the smallest input sufficient to elicit a specified response. Krasne and colleagues repeatedly stimulated an abdominal sensory nerve while recording LG-related activity in adult _Procambarus clarkii_ during rest and paired interaction.

Test shocks lasted 0.2 ms. The researchers varied shock strength to estimate the level needed to trigger LG, while also monitoring upstream sensory interneuron activity. This separated availability of the giant reflex from the number of spontaneous escapes during an encounter.

LG thresholds increased during agonistic activity, especially in subordinates. A higher threshold means stronger experimental input was needed to release the stereotyped reflex. Electrical nerve stimulation bypasses part of natural stimulus transduction, so its voltage does not directly specify the force of an opponent’s contact or the probability of every escape type.

slides.title: Interaction suppresses LG more strongly in subordinates
body: Krasne and colleagues compared each animal before, during and after social interaction. Thresholds were normalized to the animal’s own resting value, allowing the effect of an encounter to be distinguished from stable differences in electrode placement or stimulus recruitment.

LG thresholds rose markedly in subordinates during interaction and less in dominants. At rest, reflex excitability did not consistently separate the two ranks. Some subordinate thresholds approached several times baseline, then fell after interaction ended.

The same subordinate can consequently retain an available LG reflex while resting and suppress it during a predictable social threat. This context dependence differs from a permanent loss of the neuron. The experiment established modulation during encounters, but did not measure serotonin release or prove that serotonin produced the observed suppression.

slides.title: Sensory excitation reaches LG by converging pathways
body: Abdominal mechanosensory afferents excite LG directly and through sensory interneurons. A **monosynaptic** pathway contains one synaptic connection; a **disynaptic** pathway contains two. A synapse is a site of signal transfer between neurons.

Edwards and colleagues combined identified-cell recordings with stained-neuron reconstructions in adult crayfish. **Interneuron A** overlaps the LG dendritic region and contributes sensory excitation. Nerve shocks produce an early α depolarization followed by a later β component reflecting interneuronal recruitment.

An **excitatory postsynaptic potential** (EPSP) is an input-evoked voltage change favoring neuronal firing. Responses are calibrated in mV and ms, separating signal size from timing. Convergence permits multiple inputs to approach LG firing threshold, but anatomical overlap alone cannot establish a functional synapse or determine which input controls behavior in every context.

slides.title: Electrical synapses depend on the voltage difference
body: An **electrical synapse** passes current between coupled neurons. **Rectification** means that transmission depends on the direction and voltage difference across the connection. It permits strong forward transmission without equivalent transfer in the opposite direction.

Edwards and colleagues recorded LG and identified sensory interneurons while injecting current to change membrane potential. Shifting postsynaptic LG voltage altered the transmitted response even when the presynaptic stimulus was retained. Their recordings resolved transferred signals on millisecond time scales.

Postsynaptic voltage therefore changes the effectiveness of incoming electrical excitation. This is distinct from changing transmitter release at a chemical synapse. The measured rectification constrains how neuromodulation can alter sensory gain, but it does not identify a serotonin receptor or a particular molecular gap-junction protein responsible for the social-status effect.

slides.title: Postsynaptic depolarization can reduce incoming EPSPs
body: A cell’s **membrane potential** is the voltage inside relative to outside. Its effect on firing depends both on proximity to spike threshold and on the transmission of its inputs. Depolarization does not necessarily enlarge every incoming synaptic response.

Edwards and colleagues shifted LG voltage by intracellular current injection while retaining sensory nerve stimulation. Across α, β and later components, hyperpolarizing LG increased EPSP amplitude, whereas depolarizing it reduced amplitude. The plotted membrane shifts span tens of mV relative to rest.

Rectifying electrical contacts provide a mechanism for this postsynaptic control of input effectiveness. The result cautions against equating depolarization with enhanced sensory gain. It establishes voltage-dependent transmission in this preparation, but the total effect on escape also depends on spike threshold, inhibition and the actual pattern of afferent excitation.

slides.title: Serotonin dose does not determine its effect alone
body: Teshiba and colleagues systematically varied serotonin concentration, onset rate and exposure duration in crayfish isolated for at least two weeks. These controls tested why different laboratories had reported opposite effects on LG.

slides.title: Slow onset favors facilitation at a high concentration
body: **Onset rate** describes how rapidly exposure reaches its final level. Teshiba and colleagues compared a rapid serotonin increase with a gradual rise to the same high condition while repeatedly measuring LG sensory EPSPs.

A slowly developing facilitatory effect can dominate before a higher-threshold inhibitory action becomes substantial. slides.title: Social experience can reverse serotonin’s effect
body: Yeh, Fricke and Edwards compared socially isolated, dominant and subordinate crayfish using bath-applied serotonin. Animals were assigned rank from repeated social behavior and paired for at least 12 days before mature status-dependent responses were evaluated.

Serotonin at 50 µM enhanced LG sensory responses in isolates and dominants, but reduced them in subordinates. Saline wash removed the effect in paired animals, whereas facilitation in isolates could persist for hours. The same identified neuron and input pathway were tested across social conditions.

A transmitter’s action therefore depends on the animal’s prior social experience. The study measured responses to experimentally supplied serotonin; it did not measure endogenous release during fighting. It supports plasticity in serotonergic modulation without establishing that this plasticity alone causes the immediate behavioral decision to withdraw.

slides.title: Equal serotonin treatment yields opposite sensory gains
body: Yeh and colleagues expanded the social-history comparison using identified LG recordings across a range of sensory shock strengths. **Subthreshold input** evokes a response without a spike; **suprathreshold input** is sufficient to initiate firing.

After 45 min of 50 µM serotonin superfusion, LG EPSPs increased across stimulus levels in isolates and dominants and decreased in established subordinates. Representative stimulus-response relations changed by about +117%, +39% and −37%, respectively. These are individual examples, not universal effect sizes.

The stimulus needed to fire LG consequently fell with facilitation and rose with inhibition. A 1-h saline wash restored paired animals toward baseline. slides.title: Input resistance changes accompany social modulation
body: **Input resistance** describes the voltage change produced by an injected current. Ion channels are membrane proteins that provide paths for ionic current. Higher resistance can permit a given input current to produce a larger voltage response; lower resistance permits more current to leave the membrane locally.

Yeh and colleagues measured LG at its initial axon segment before serotonin, during exposure and after a 1-h wash. Isolates and dominants displayed small depolarizations and increased input resistance; subordinates displayed hyperpolarization and reduced resistance. The changes accompanied their opposite EPSP responses.

The association supports modulation of LG membrane properties, rather than only changing sensory recruitment. Measurement at the axon segment does not fully reveal conductance distribution across all dendrites. These recordings also do not identify the ion-channel species responsible or prove that one resistance change explains every effect on electrical synaptic input.

slides.title: Subordinate modulation develops over days and reverses

slides.title: Promotion changes the previously subordinate response
body: Yeh and colleagues paired former subordinates with one another, allowing one member to acquire dominant status. This manipulation tested whether a retained inhibitory serotonin response could change after a new social relationship developed.

Promotion therefore changes an experienced subordinate’s cellular modulation on a multi-day time scale. slides.title: Repeated input habituates the LG response
body: **Habituation** is a decline in response during repeated stimulation. Araki and colleagues tested isolated abdominal nerve cords from adult crayfish, stimulating sensory roots while recording whether LG produced an action potential. The preparation preserved the local sensory pathway while removing ongoing social interaction.

Just-suprathreshold shocks were delivered every 5 s. In control saline, response probability fell rapidly, with roughly half the preparations failing within the first five trials. Pretreatment with 10 µM serotonin or octopamine slowed the decline.

The amines increased the number of stimuli needed to lose reliable LG firing. This establishes modulation of repeated-input responsiveness, rather than a measured change in free-animal retreat or fighting. Because the initial stimulus was selected near threshold, a modest increase in sensory gain can strongly affect whether a repeated trial still recruits the giant neuron.

body: A **second-messenger analogue** is a compound designed to activate or mimic part of an intracellular signaling pathway. Araki and colleagues compared cyclic-nucleotide analogues after establishing a near-threshold stimulus to the LG sensory pathway.

The retained difference supports a local functional reconfiguration induced by social experience. It does not show that higher centers were irrelevant when the change originally developed. Nor does it establish that this local walking circuit uses the same receptors or intracellular mechanism that modulate the LG escape command neuron.

slides.title: One serotonin neuron produces mixed motor effects
body: Bacqué-Cazenave and colleagues activated an identified serotonin neuron in the first abdominal ganglion of socially isolated adult crayfish. Intracellular current pulses drove the cell while the researchers recorded individual walking-leg motor units and motor-neuron voltage.

A 10-s activation produced excitation in some units, inhibition in others and little change in others. In the same recording, one depressor neuron depolarized while another unit in its nerve reduced its discharge. Changes in the average nerve activity could conceal these opposing effects.

Activation of an endogenous modulatory cell therefore does not impose one uniform sign on its targets. The result extends beyond experiments applying serotonin to a bath. It concerns the walking-leg network in isolated animals and does not prove that the same neuron generates status-dependent LG inhibition or controls the decision to retreat during fighting.

slides.title: Motor modulation changes resistance and EPSPs
body: The effect of serotonin-cell activation can be examined at a single postsynaptic motor neuron. Bacqué-Cazenave and colleagues combined current injection with controlled movement of the **coxo-basal chordotonal organ**, a proprioceptor that senses movement at a walking-leg joint.

Excited depressor neurons depolarized and increased input resistance, while inhibited neurons hyperpolarized and decreased resistance. Sensory EPSPs became larger or smaller accordingly. The recordings retained mV calibration and included current pulses of known amplitude to estimate resistance.

Opposing membrane and synaptic effects connect modulation to sensory-motor output at identified targets. They are consistent with different receptor actions or receptor distributions, but do not by themselves identify the molecular subtype on each cell. These motor-neuron measurements also cannot replace direct tests of the giant escape system or of fighting behavior.

slides.title: Previous success and amines alter later contest outcomes
body: A **winner effect** is increased success after a previous victory; a **loser effect** is reduced success after defeat. Momohara and colleagues paired adult male crayfish with modest size differences, then tested experienced animals against unfamiliar opponents on the following day.

Previously successful smaller animals won about 70% of later pairings against larger naive opponents. Previously defeated larger animals won only about 6% against smaller naive animals. Serotonin injection into naive smaller animals also increased winning to over 60% under the tested conditions.

Experience and pharmacological treatment can therefore outweigh a modest physical advantage. The injected serotonin solution was 1–2 µM, distinct from a measured tissue concentration. These outcomes do not identify the LG circuit as the cause of winning or establish that endogenous serotonin alone carries the full memory of victory.

slides.title: Drug effects depend on social history and treatment timing
body: **Fluoxetine** inhibits serotonin uptake, reducing its removal into cells. Huber and colleagues found that co-treatment with fluoxetine reduced the fighting-duration increase caused by infused serotonin in established subordinates. Acute fluoxetine alone did not produce the same persistence increase.

Momohara and colleagues instead treated animals after they acquired dominance and tested a new encounter on the following day. Fluoxetine reinforced the winner effect, whereas the serotonin antagonist mianserin reduced it. These protocols differed in species, previous rank and timing.

The outcomes are not interchangeable measures of a universal aggression mechanism. One tested an acute serotonin-dependent change during an ongoing size-asymmetric relationship; the other tested subsequent contest success after experience. Uptake-related pharmacology supports serotonin involvement, but neither experiment identifies every affected receptor or the relevant circuit.

slides.title: Defeat can increase avoidance after the encounter
body: Bacqué-Cazenave and colleagues tested **anxiety-like behavior**, operationally defined as increased avoidance of illuminated maze arms and more retreats at dark-light boundaries. Male crayfish were paired for 20 min, then tested individually rather than measuring escape during the fight.

Losers avoided light more than winners and isolated controls. Continued attacks after defeat predicted avoidance more closely than fight duration. Pretreatment with methysergide, a serotonin antagonist, increased time in light arms from roughly 20% to 40% in subsequent losers while reducing boundary retreats.

The drug-treated animals could still lose and withdraw, separating later avoidance from the initial decision to retreat. The assay supports a serotonin-associated effect of social stress, but does not identify a giant escape-neuron mechanism or establish a human subjective emotional state from behavior alone.

items.text: Dominance changes the balance of attacks, retreats and escape types. Frequent subordinate escape does not imply frequent lateral giant activation.
LG excitability during interaction differs from excitability at rest. Serotonin’s effect depends on past rank, current experience and drug-delivery conditions.
Subordinate serotonin inhibition develops after the initial behavioral decision and can reverse after isolation. Previous dominance can persist in LG modulation after demotion.
Rectifying electrical inputs and membrane conductance contribute to LG responsiveness. cAMP interventions support a postsynaptic facilitatory pathway in the tested preparation.
Agonist effects, cloned-receptor signaling and immunostaining answer different questions. The mapped type-1 receptor was not detected on LG; its direct role there is unproven.
Fighting persistence, contest success, walking-leg orientation and post-defeat avoidance are distinct outcomes. Serotonin does not impose a single sign across all cells or behaviors.
